McLaren: McLaren’s aero package this weekend gets a modest makeover: the floor’s shape has been tweaked to smooth out airflow, the rear‑suspension cover has been reshaped for cleaner air, and a fresh rear wing design adds a bit more bite. Together they give the car extra grip and stability, especially in high‑speed corners, so drivers can push harder and keep the tyres in their sweet spot. In short, the tweaks should translate into better cornering confidence and a stronger fight for podium positions.
Mercedes F1 Team: Mercedes has re‑shaped the R01’s sidepods to funnel more air down the car and fitted a bigger inlet, giving extra grip in the corners. The front wing now leans more aggressively and the little vertical fences have been dropped, while the rear wing sits at a steeper angle – both changes are designed to squeeze out more downforce without adding much drag. In short, the car should stick to the tarmac better, helping the drivers attack the slower bends and defend their positions this weekend.
Racing Bulls / RB: Racing Bulls has reshaped almost every aero surface to fit the new 2026 rulebook – the front and rear wings, nose, floor and even the engine‑cover now have slimmer, longer profiles and a revised layout that trims down the car’s overall wing area. These changes give the car a cleaner airflow and a more predictable balance, meaning drivers will have a tighter corner‑entry feel and a stronger straight‑line push, but they’ll also need to adapt to the revised down‑force levels this weekend. In short, the car is sleeker and more efficient, so getting the new setup right could be the difference between fighting for points or staying at the back of the pack.
Aston Martin: Aston Martin has gone slimmer and sharper up front – a three‑element, narrow wing with a new dive‑plane endplate and a higher, more separated nose – giving the car quicker turn‑in and better stability through the corners. The side‑pod inlets are now higher and point straight at the on‑track airflow, while the undercut that runs from the side‑pods all the way to the rear is deeper and the roof slopes down, funneling cooling air more efficiently and cleaning the airflow to a three‑element rear wing that produces extra rear grip. In short, the package is all about sharper front end response and a stronger, more stable rear end, which should translate into faster laps and more consistent tyre performance this weekend.
Haas F1 Team: Haas has reshaped the underside of the car with a new‑style diffuser, giving a noticeable boost in downforce that should help the car stick to the track through the fast corners. The rear wing now features a three‑piece upper element packed into a tighter box, adding extra grip without breaking the rules, while the beam wing has been stripped back to a single, simpler piece. Together these tweaks aim to improve stability and cornering speed for this weekend’s race, giving the team a better chance to fight for higher positions.
Alpine F1 Team: Alpine has rolled out an all‑new front wing and rear wing that meet the fresh 2026 rulebook, plus a revamped engine‑cover “coke” to smooth the airflow over the car. The new wings should give the car more usable down‑force and stability in corners, while the updated bodywork reduces drag and helps the car breathe better on the straights. In short, these aero tweaks are aimed at faster lap times and a stronger fight for position this weekend.
Audi F1 Team: Audi’s new front wing now has independent micro‑actuators on each side, letting the team fine‑tune the airflow on the fly and keep the car balanced through corners. The side‑pod inlet and its “down‑wash” shaping have been re‑sculpted to work hand‑in‑hand with the floor and rear body, feeding cleaner air to the rear and generating extra grip. Together, these tweaks should give the Audi a steadier, more planted feel around the circuit, especially in the twisty sections of this weekend’s race.
Cadillac: Cadillac has reshaped the front‑wing flap, its end‑plates and the rear wing to fine‑tune how the aero load is spread across the car, giving it a smoother, more predictable push. The result is extra bite in the corners and a steadier rear end, so drivers can push harder on lap 1 without fighting sudden instability. In short, the tweaks should translate into quicker corner exits and a more consistent feel throughout the race weekend.
